TEST CASES: PRIMER DESIGN (version 1)
======================================
Designer: journal/primer_design.py
Tests:    journal/test_primer_design.py
Run:      python3 journal/test_primer_design.py   (12 cases, about 4 s)
Real-data check: CDC N1/N2/N3 (see the end of this file)

The designer takes a genome, a target gene inside it and a mismatch
allowance (0-2), and returns up to 3 designs: a 20-base forward primer, a
20-base reverse primer and a 24-base probe. It uses only what the first model
uses (sequence, mismatch allowance, binding sites on both strands, product
length, probe inside the product), plus GC content. No melting or annealing
temperature.

Fake genome (the same every run: seeded random bases):
  2,000 random bases (seed 1, 50 % GC)
  + 400-base target (seed 3, 45.3 % GC)
  + 2,000 random bases (seed 2, 50 % GC)
  Target = genome positions 2001-2400 (1-based)
  Target starts GCATGCTGGTAGGTTTCAACCTCTTAATAATGTGGCAGCTAGGTCGTGTCATGTTATGCT...

Rules every returned design must follow (checked for every design):
  - forward = the genome window; reverse = reverse complement of its window;
    probe = the genome window
  - primers 20 bases, probe 24 bases, all inside the target
  - probe between the primers, overlapping neither
  - product 60-150 bp
  - no oligo above 70 % GC
  - independent check: run_model (first model) on the whole genome with the
    designed oligos finds exactly ONE product, status "product", at the
    designed place

Ranking: fewest medium-GC oligos, then product closest to 100 bp, then
earliest start. Each later design's product must not overlap an earlier one.

GC bands (target and each oligo):
  ok        up to 60 %
  medium    above 60 %, up to 70 %   -> warning; oligo still usable
  too high  above 70 %               -> target: error, stops before the search
                                        oligo: never used

Positions below are 1-based (genome position 1 = first base).


CASES THAT SHOULD GIVE DESIGNS
------------------------------

Case 1 - Basic: 400-base target in a 4,400-base genome
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  target found at 2001-2400, + strand; 3 designs, no warnings
    Design 1  F 5'-GCATGCTGGTAGGTTTCAAC-3'      2001-2020
              R 5'-CATAGTACGGAGAATACCCA-3'      binds 2081-2100
              P 5'-CTAGGTCGTGTCATGTTATGCTTA-3'  2039-2062
              product 2001-2100, 100 bp
    Design 2  F 5'-GTAACGTGCTAGGCAATCCC-3'      2101-2120
              R 5'-ATTTATTTGTGGTGAAAAGC-3'      binds 2181-2200
              P 5'-CTCACAAGTTGTTAAAAATGGGTA-3'  2139-2162
              product 2101-2200, 100 bp
    Design 3  F 5'-TGCGCTCTCCATCCCCCTTT-3'      2204-2223
              R 5'-CTTCTGGTTGGAGAGGATAC-3'      binds 2284-2303
              P 5'-CTGGGAGTAAAAATATTCTTGAGT-3'  2242-2265
              product 2204-2303, 100 bp
  Meaning:  Every rule holds and the first model agrees each design gives
            only one product. The 3 products do not overlap. (Design 3
            starts at 2204, not 2201: the windows starting 2201-2203 were
            not unique or not usable.)

Case 2 - The first design, worked out by hand
  Allowance: 2
  Worked:   Best = product closest to 100 bp, then earliest start, so the
            forward primer starts at the target's first base, 2001.
            Product 2001-2100 -> reverse window 2081-2100.
            Gap between primers = 2021-2080 (60 bases).
            Probe (24) centred: 2021 + (60 - 24) // 2 = 2039 -> 2039-2062.
  Outcome:  forward 2001, reverse 2081-2100, probe 2039, product 100 bp
  Meaning:  The ranking and probe placement do what the code says.

Case 3 - Target given as its reverse complement
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  target found on the - strand at 2001-2400; same 3 designs as
            Case 1
  Meaning:  A gene can be pasted from either strand.

Case 4 - Genome and target pasted as FASTA, lowercase, 60 bases per line
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  same 3 designs as Case 1
  Meaning:  ">" header lines, line breaks and lowercase letters are cleaned
            away before the search.

Case 5 - 30 N bases in the middle of the target (target 181-210 = N)
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  3 designs, products 2001-2100, 2219-2318, 2101-2180;
            no primer or probe contains N
  Meaning:  Missing data is never put into an oligo (the first model would
            call such a site "not assessable"). Design 3 is shorter (80 bp)
            because the N block cuts into the space after 2180.

Case 6 - A 40-base all-G/C stretch inside an ordinary target
  (target 101-140 replaced by random G/C, genome 2101-2140)
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  target GC 50.5 % (ok overall); 3 designs, products 2001-2100,
            2133-2232, 2233-2332; the highest oligo GC is 60 %
  Meaning:  A GC-rich patch is skipped even when the target as a whole is
            fine: no oligo above 70 % GC is used.


SPECIFICITY (the first model's job)
-----------------------------------

Case 7 - The target appears twice in the genome
  (genome = Case 1 genome + a second exact copy of the target at the end)
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  no design; all 25,578 possible designs checked, every one fails
  Meaning:  Every primer binds both copies, so no design is specific.

Case 8 - A second copy with every 10th base changed (A->C, C->G, G->T, T->A)
  Worked:   Any 20 bases in a row cover exactly 2 changed bases (one in
            every 10), so every primer matches the copy with 2 mismatches.
  Allowance 2:  no design (every primer also binds the copy)
  Allowance 1:  3 designs, products 2001-2100, 2101-2200, 2204-2303 (the
                same as Case 1), all passing every rule
  Meaning:  The mismatch allowance decides what counts as an off-target
            site, exactly as in the first model.


GC CONTENT
----------

Case 9 - Target 80 % GC (400 random bases, seed 9)
  Outcome:  ERROR: the target's GC content is 80.0 %, above 70 %: primers
            here would bind too strongly, also at partly matching sites, and
            the GC-rich template folds on itself and copies poorly. Choose a
            less GC-rich target.

Case 10 - GC-rich target that is NOT in the genome (seed 10, 80.2 % GC)
  Outcome:  the GC error above, not "the target gene is not in the genome"
  Meaning:  The GC check really runs first, before the target is even
            looked up.

Case 11 - Target 65.5 % GC (seed 11)
  Outcome:  WARNING: target GC content is 65.5 % (medium, above 60 %):
            primers may bind more strongly than intended; check the designs
            before ordering
            3 designs still returned, products 2038-2137, 2310-2400,
            2185-2256; none uses a medium-GC oligo, so no per-oligo
            warnings
  Meaning:  A medium target is a warning, not an error, and the ranking
            picks ok-GC oligos when there are any.
  Not yet tested: a design that has to use a medium-GC oligo (and gets its
            own "design n: ... GC content is ... (medium)" warning).


BAD INPUT
---------

Case 12 - Errors with a reason
  Target not in the genome  -> the target gene is not in the genome
                               (checked both strands)
  Allowance 3               -> mismatch allowance must be 0 to 2
  Allowance -1              -> mismatch allowance must be 0 to 2
  59-base target            -> the target must be at least 60 bases long


REAL DATA: CDC N1/N2/N3 ON THE REFERENCE GENOME (not in the test file yet)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Genome:   NC_045512.2 (29,903 bases), allowance 2
  Target:   the published product plus 50 bases on each side

  (a) Do the published primers and probe pass the designer's rules?

  Assay  Product        Sites per oligo  GC F / R / P (%)     Result
  N1     28287-28358    1 / 1 / 1        45.0 / 45.8 / 58.3   pass
  N2     29164-29230    1 / 1 / 1        40.0 / 55.6 / 56.5   pass
  N3     28681-28752    1 / 1 / 1        45.5 / 47.6 / 56.5   pass, but the
                                                              probe has a Y,
                                                              which the
                                                              designer never
                                                              proposes

  (b) Does the designer reproduce them?  No.

  Assay  Published                          Designer's first choice
  N1     F 28287-28306, R 28335-28358, 72   F 28237-28256, R 28317-28336, 100
  N2     F 29164-29183, R 29213-29230, 67   F 29118-29137, R 29198-29217, 100
  N3     F 28681-28702, R 28732-28752, 72   F 28631-28650, R 28711-28730, 100

  Why: the designer only makes 20-base primers and 24-base probes (the CDC
  used 18-24 and 23-24), and it prefers 100 bp products starting at the
  target's first base (the CDC products are 67-72 bp). Its designs also pass
  the specificity check: with only first-model information, many designs
  are equally good.

    Design 3  F 5'-TGCGCTCTCCATCCCCCTTT-3'      2204-2223
              R 5'-CTTCTGGTTGGAGAGGATAC-3'      binds 2284-2303
              P 5'-CTGGGAGTAAAAATATTCTTGAGT-3'  2242-2265
              product 2204-2303, 100 bp
  Meaning:  Every rule holds and the first model agrees each design gives
            only one product. The 3 products do not overlap. (Design 3
            starts at 2204, not 2201: the windows starting 2201-2203 were
            not unique or not usable.)

Case 2 - The first design, worked out by hand
  Allowance: 2
  Worked:   Best = product closest to 100 bp, then earliest start, so the
            forward primer starts at the target's first base, 2001.
            Product 2001-2100 -> reverse window 2081-2100.
            Gap between primers = 2021-2080 (60 bases).
            Probe (24) centred: 2021 + (60 - 24) // 2 = 2039 -> 2039-2062.
  Outcome:  forward 2001, reverse 2081-2100, probe 2039, product 100 bp
  Meaning:  The ranking and probe placement do what the code says.

Case 3 - Target given as its reverse complement
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  target found on the - strand at 2001-2400; same 3 designs as
            Case 1
  Meaning:  A gene can be pasted from either strand.

Case 4 - Genome and target pasted as FASTA, lowercase, 60 bases per line
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  same 3 designs as Case 1
  Meaning:  ">" header lines, line breaks and lowercase letters are cleaned
            away before the search.

Case 5 - 30 N bases in the middle of the target (target 181-210 = N)
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  3 designs, products 2001-2100, 2219-2318, 2101-2180;
            no primer or probe contains N
  Meaning:  Missing data is never put into an oligo (the first model would
            call such a site "not assessable"). Design 3 is shorter (80 bp)
            because the N block cuts into the space after 2180.

Case 6 - A 40-base all-G/C stretch inside an ordinary target
  (target 101-140 replaced by random G/C, genome 2101-2140)
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  target GC 50.5 % (ok overall); 3 designs, products 2001-2100,
            2133-2232, 2233-2332; the highest oligo GC is 60 %
  Meaning:  A GC-rich patch is skipped even when the target as a whole is
            fine: no oligo above 70 % GC is used.


SPECIFICITY (the first model's job)
-----------------------------------

Case 7 - The target appears twice in the genome
  (genome = Case 1 genome + a second exact copy of the target at the end)
  Allowance: 2
  Outcome:  no design; all 25,578 possible designs checked, every one fails
  Meaning:  Every primer binds both copies, so no design is specific.

Case 8 - A second copy with every 10th base changed (A->C, C->G, G->T, T->A)
  Worked:   Any 20 bases in a row cover exactly 2 changed bases (one in
            every 10), so every primer matches the copy with 2 mismatches.
  Allowance 2:  no design (every primer also binds the copy)
  Allowance 1:  3 designs, products 2001-2100, 2101-2200, 2204-2303 (the

  Meaning:  The mismatch allowance decides what counts as an off-target
            site, exactly as in the first model.

----------

Case 9 - Target 80 % GC (400 random bases, seed 9)
  Outcome:  ERROR: the target's GC content is 80.0 %, above 70 %: primers
            here would bind too strongly, also at partly matching sites, and
            the GC-rich template folds on itself and copies poorly. Choose a
            less GC-rich target.

Case 10 - GC-rich target that is NOT in the genome (seed 10, 80.2 % GC)
  Outcome:  the GC error above, not "the target gene is not in the genome"
  Meaning:  The GC check really runs first, before the target is even

  Outcome:  WARNING: target GC content is 65.5 % (medium, above 60 %):

            before ordering
            3 designs still returned, products 2038-2137, 2310-2400,
            2185-2256; none uses a medium-GC oligo, so no per-oligo
            warnings
  Meaning:  A medium target is a warning, not an error, and the ranking
            picks ok-GC oligos when there are any.

            own "design n: ... GC content is ... (medium)" warning).

Case 12 - Errors with a reason
  Target not in the genome  -> the target gene is not in the genome

  Allowance 3               -> mismatch allowance must be 0 to 2
  Allowance -1              -> mismatch allowance must be 0 to 2
  59-base target            -> the target must be at least 60 bases long

  Genome:   NC_045512.2 (29,903 bases), allowance 2
  Target:   the published product plus 50 bases on each side

  Assay  Product        Sites per oligo  GC F / R / P (%)     Result
  N1     28287-28358    1 / 1 / 1        45.0 / 45.8 / 58.3   pass
  N2     29164-29230    1 / 1 / 1        40.0 / 55.6 / 56.5   pass
  N3     28681-28752    1 / 1 / 1        45.5 / 47.6 / 56.5   pass, but the
                                                              probe has a Y,
                                                              which the
                                                              designer never
                                                              proposes

  (b) Does the designer reproduce them?  No.

  Assay  Published                          Designer's first choice
  N1     F 28287-28306, R 28335-28358, 72   F 28237-28256, R 28317-28336, 100
  N2     F 29164-29183, R 29213-29230, 67   F 29118-29137, R 29198-29217, 100
  N3     F 28681-28702, R 28732-28752, 72   F 28631-28650, R 28711-28730, 100

  Why: the designer only makes 20-base primers and 24-base probes (the CDC
  used 18-24 and 23-24), and it prefers 100 bp products starting at the
  target's first base (the CDC products are 67-72 bp). Its designs also pass
  the specificity check: with only first-model information, many designs

## Log 11 · 2026-11-13 · Primer design from the first model

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

### What I did
- Started on a website idea: paste a genome, a target gene and a mismatch
  allowance, and get back primers and a probe. Before building the website,
  I made the code that does the designing, `primer_design.py`.
- The first model *checks* primers someone else designed. This one goes the
  other way: it *designs* a forward primer, a reverse primer and a probe for
  a target gene, then uses the first model to check them **(#47)**.
- I kept it to what the first model knows: the sequence, the mismatch
  allowance, where things bind on both strands, the product length, and the
  probe being inside the product. No melting or annealing temperature. A
  first draft borrowed Tm from the second model, and I took it out
  **(#47)**.
- How it designs: every 20-base stretch of the target can be a forward
  primer, and its reverse complement a reverse primer. Pairs that make a
  60-150 bp product get a 24-base probe in the middle. A design is kept only
  if each primer and the probe stick in exactly one place on the whole
  genome, and the first model finds just the one product **(#47)**.
- The first three designs were the same pair shifted by one base, so now
  the designs can't overlap each other **(#48)**.
- Added GC content, because G-C pairs hold on with three bonds and A-T with
  two, so GC-rich primers stick too hard, even where they only partly
  match. The target's GC is checked first, before anything else runs: above
  70% the program stops and says why; 60-70% it carries on with a warning.
  Each primer and probe gets the same bands: above 70% is never used, and
  60-70% is used but flagged **(#49)**.
- GC was rounded to whole numbers, so 69.6% printed as "70 %" next to the
  word "medium". Now it shows one decimal **(#50)**.
- Ran 12 fake-genome test cases (`test_primer_design.py`); all pass. The
  first run failed once, but the bug was in my test: it counted the target
  warning as a primer warning because both contain the word "design"
  **(#51)**.
- Tried the CDC N1, N2 and N3 primers. They all pass the designer's rules:
  one site each, one product, probe inside, GC 40-58%. But the designer
  does not come up with them. It only makes 20-base primers and likes
  100 bp products; the CDC used 18-24 bases and 67-72 bp products
  **(#52)**.

## Log 11 · 2026-11-13 · Primer design from the first model

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

**#47. Problem:** the models only check existing primers. For the planned
website, a user should be able to give a genome, a target gene and a
mismatch allowance and get primers back.
**Fix:** new `primer_design.py`, `design_primers(genome, target,
max_mismatches)`:
1. `clean_sequence` accepts plain or FASTA text (drops `>` lines,
   whitespace, lowercase); `find_target` finds the target on either strand.
2. `possible_designs`: every `PRIMER_LENGTH` = 20 window of the target with
   known bases only (`KNOWN_BASES`) is a forward primer; its reverse
   complement is a reverse primer. Pairs giving `PRODUCT_LENGTH` = 60-150 bp
   get a `PROBE_LENGTH` = 24 probe centred in the gap. Sorted by product
   length closest to `IDEAL_PRODUCT` = 100, then start.
3. `specific`: each oligo must have exactly one site from
   `find_binding_sites` on the whole genome (one shared k-mer index, results
   cached per oligo), then `run_model` must give exactly one product, status
   "product", at the designed coordinates.

`MAX_ALLOWED_MISMATCHES` = 2: with k = 6, `find_binding_sites` needs
length // (allowance + 1) >= 6, so 20-base primers allow at most 2 (#15,
#40). Output: 5'-forward-3', 3'-reverse-5' (written backwards to line up
under the genome) and the order sequence, binding positions (1-based),
lengths, product, probe position.

The first draft also filtered on Tm (58-62 C, probe 6-12 C above, via the
second model's `perfect_tm`), GC 40-60% and base runs. All of it was removed
so the designer uses first-model information only.

**#48. Problem:** the three designs returned were one pair shifted by one
base (2-4 products all overlapping).
**Fix:** a design is skipped if its product overlaps an already chosen one.

**#49. Problem:** with first-model information only, nearly every window
passes, including GC-rich ones that bind too strongly and mis-prime.
**Fix:** Section 2b, `gc_fraction` (known bases only, so N does not lower
it) and `gc_level`: ok <= 60% (`GC_MEDIUM_ABOVE`), medium <= 70%
(`GC_TOO_HIGH_ABOVE`), too high above that.
- `check_target_gc` runs first in `design_primers`, after the input checks
  and before `find_target`: too high raises `ValueError` with the GC value
  and the reason; medium adds a warning.
- `usable` excludes oligos above 70%. Medium-GC oligos are kept, listed in
  each design's `medium_gc`, and get one warning each.
- Sort key is now (number of medium-GC oligos, product distance from 100,
  start), so ok-GC designs come first.
- The command line prints `ERROR: ...` and exits 1 on a `ValueError`.

**#50. Problem:** `gc_percent` rounded to whole numbers, so a 69.6% target
printed as "70 %" while labelled medium.
**Fix:** one decimal place.

**#51. Tests** (`test_primer_design.py`, cases in
`test_cases_primer_design.txt`): a 4,400-base seeded random genome with a
400-base target at 2001-2400. Every returned design is checked against all
the rules and by an independent `run_model` call. 12 cases: basic, first
design by hand (F 2001, R 2081-2100, probe 2039, 100 bp), reverse-complement
target, FASTA input, N block, GC-rich patch, two copies (no design), a near
copy with every 10th base changed (no design at allowance 2, 3 at
allowance 1), 80% GC target (error), 80% GC target missing from the genome
(GC error first), 65.5% GC target (warning) and bad input. All pass.
The first run failed in Case 11: the test counted warnings containing
"design", and the target warning contains "designs". Fixed in the test
(`startswith("design ")`); the designer was unchanged.

**#52. Result: CDC N1/N2/N3** on NC_045512.2, target = published product
+/- 50 bases, allowance 2:
- The published oligos pass every designer rule: 1 site each, one product,
  probe inside, GC 40.0-58.3%. The N3 probe has a Y, which the designer
  never proposes (known bases only).
- The designer does not reproduce them. Its first choices are 100 bp
  products starting at the target's first base (e.g. N1: F 28237-28256,
  R 28317-28336) vs the published 67-72 bp. Causes: fixed 20/24-base
  lengths (CDC: 18-24 / 23-24) and `IDEAL_PRODUCT` = 100.

## Log 11 · 2026-11-13 · Primer design from the first model

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

### What I did
- Started on a website idea: paste a genome, a target gene and a mismatch
  allowance, and get back primers and a probe. Before building the website,
  I made the code that does the designing, `primer_design.py`.
- The first model *checks* primers someone else designed. This one goes the
  other way: it *designs* a forward primer, a reverse primer and a probe for
  a target gene, then uses the first model to check them **(#47)**.
- I kept it to what the first model knows: the sequence, the mismatch
  allowance, where things bind on both strands, the product length, and the
  probe being inside the product. No melting or annealing temperature. A
  first draft borrowed Tm from the second model, and I took it out
  **(#47)**.
- How it designs: every 20-base stretch of the target can be a forward
  primer, and its reverse complement a reverse primer. Pairs that make a
  60-150 bp product get a 24-base probe in the middle. A design is kept only
  if each primer and the probe stick in exactly one place on the whole
  genome, and the first model finds just the one product **(#47)**.
- The first three designs were the same pair shifted by one base, so now
  the designs can't overlap each other **(#48)**.
- Added GC content, because G-C pairs hold on with three bonds and A-T with
  two, so GC-rich primers stick too hard, even where they only partly
  match. The target's GC is checked first, before anything else runs: above
  70% the program stops and says why; 60-70% it carries on with a warning.
  Each primer and probe gets the same bands: above 70% is never used, and
  60-70% is used but flagged **(#49)**.
- GC was rounded to whole numbers, so 69.6% printed as "70 %" next to the
  word "medium". Now it shows one decimal **(#50)**.
- Ran 12 fake-genome test cases (`test_primer_design.py`); all pass. The
  first run failed once, but the bug was in my test: it counted the target
  warning as a primer warning because both contain the word "design"
  **(#51)**.
- Tried the CDC N1, N2 and N3 primers. They all pass the designer's rules:
  one site each, one product, probe inside, GC 40-58%. But the designer
  does not come up with them. It only makes 20-base primers and likes
  100 bp products; the CDC used 18-24 bases and 67-72 bp products
  **(#52)**.

## Log 11 · 2026-11-13 · Primer design from the first model

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

**#47. Problem:** the models only check existing primers. For the planned
website, a user should be able to give a genome, a target gene and a
mismatch allowance and get primers back.
**Fix:** new `primer_design.py`, `design_primers(genome, target,
max_mismatches)`:
1. `clean_sequence` accepts plain or FASTA text (drops `>` lines,
   whitespace, lowercase); `find_target` finds the target on either strand.
2. `possible_designs`: every `PRIMER_LENGTH` = 20 window of the target with
   known bases only (`KNOWN_BASES`) is a forward primer; its reverse
   complement is a reverse primer. Pairs giving `PRODUCT_LENGTH` = 60-150 bp
   get a `PROBE_LENGTH` = 24 probe centred in the gap. Sorted by product
   length closest to `IDEAL_PRODUCT` = 100, then start.
3. `specific`: each oligo must have exactly one site from
   `find_binding_sites` on the whole genome (one shared k-mer index, results
   cached per oligo), then `run_model` must give exactly one product, status
   "product", at the designed coordinates.

`MAX_ALLOWED_MISMATCHES` = 2: with k = 6, `find_binding_sites` needs
length // (allowance + 1) >= 6, so 20-base primers allow at most 2 (#15,
#40). Output: 5'-forward-3', 3'-reverse-5' (written backwards to line up
under the genome) and the order sequence, binding positions (1-based),
lengths, product, probe position.

The first draft also filtered on Tm (58-62 C, probe 6-12 C above, via the
second model's `perfect_tm`), GC 40-60% and base runs. All of it was removed
so the designer uses first-model information only.

**#48. Problem:** the three designs returned were one pair shifted by one
base (2-4 products all overlapping).
**Fix:** a design is skipped if its product overlaps an already chosen one.

**#49. Problem:** with first-model information only, nearly every window
passes, including GC-rich ones that bind too strongly and mis-prime.
**Fix:** Section 2b, `gc_fraction` (known bases only, so N does not lower
it) and `gc_level`: ok <= 60% (`GC_MEDIUM_ABOVE`), medium <= 70%
(`GC_TOO_HIGH_ABOVE`), too high above that.
- `check_target_gc` runs first in `design_primers`, after the input checks
  and before `find_target`: too high raises `ValueError` with the GC value
  and the reason; medium adds a warning.
- `usable` excludes oligos above 70%. Medium-GC oligos are kept, listed in
  each design's `medium_gc`, and get one warning each.
- Sort key is now (number of medium-GC oligos, product distance from 100,
  start), so ok-GC designs come first.
- The command line prints `ERROR: ...` and exits 1 on a `ValueError`.

**#50. Problem:** `gc_percent` rounded to whole numbers, so a 69.6% target
printed as "70 %" while labelled medium.
**Fix:** one decimal place.

**#51. Tests** (`test_primer_design.py`, cases in
`test_cases_primer_design.txt`): a 4,400-base seeded random genome with a
400-base target at 2001-2400. Every returned design is checked against all
the rules and by an independent `run_model` call. 12 cases: basic, first
design by hand (F 2001, R 2081-2100, probe 2039, 100 bp), reverse-complement
target, FASTA input, N block, GC-rich patch, two copies (no design), a near
copy with every 10th base changed (no design at allowance 2, 3 at
allowance 1), 80% GC target (error), 80% GC target missing from the genome
(GC error first), 65.5% GC target (warning) and bad input. All pass.
The first run failed in Case 11: the test counted warnings containing
"design", and the target warning contains "designs". Fixed in the test
(`startswith("design ")`); the designer was unchanged.

**#52. Result: CDC N1/N2/N3** on NC_045512.2, target = published product
+/- 50 bases, allowance 2:
- The published oligos pass every designer rule: 1 site each, one product,
  probe inside, GC 40.0-58.3%. The N3 probe has a Y, which the designer
  never proposes (known bases only).
- The designer does not reproduce them. Its first choices are 100 bp
  products starting at the target's first base (e.g. N1: F 28237-28256,
  R 28317-28336) vs the published 67-72 bp. Causes: fixed 20/24-base
  lengths (CDC: 18-24 / 23-24) and `IDEAL_PRODUCT` = 100.

Hi! Welcome back. Last time we built the primer designer and pushed it to GitHub as `19b27c0`.

From the next-time list, the top items are:
- Let the designer use 18–24-base primers and aim for about 70 bp products, then see where the CDC designs rank among its options.

message.content: good primer design, but should we set a specific length for the primer? eg. between 18-30

content: or esle there would be too many choices

content.text:
Yes, a range is better than a fixed 20. I'd use **18–24 bases for primers** and **18–30 for probes** (a probe can be longer than the primers).

- **Why 18 at the bottom:** your first model needs every primer to split into at least 3 six-base seeds at the top mismatch allowance of 2. That's 3 × 6 = 18, so anything shorter breaks the search guarantee (#15, #40).
- **Why 24 at the top for primers:** that's the usual qPCR range, and it covers every CDC primer (18–24). Primers longer than about 25 are more likely to fold on themselves or stick to each other, and nothing gets better in return.
- **Why up to 30 for probes:** probes need to stay bound longer than the primers, so they're usually a few bases longer. The CDC's are 23–24, and 30 matches your existing fake test oligos.

**The catch:** a range needs a rule for picking the length. Normally Tm decides it: lengthen the primer until it reaches about 60 °C. We've left Tm out, so the designer needs another rule:

1. **GC closest to 50%:** for each start position, take the length whose GC content is nearest 50%. This uses the GC check we already have.
2. **Shortest that's still unique:** take the shortest length that binds in only one place in the genome. This is pure first-model information.
3. **Closest to 20:** a fixed preference, like now but with some flexibility.

I'd go with **option 1**. It's the closest stand-in for Tm using only what we have, since GC content is what mostly sets a primer's Tm. It also gives the CDC designs a fair chance in the ranking test.

The pairing step also needs to change. Trying every length at every position for both primers would mean millions of pairs. Picking one length per start position first keeps it about as fast as now.

Should I go ahead with 18–24 primers, 18–30 probes and the GC-closest-to-50% rule?

message.content: or esle there would be too many choices

content: yes

content.text:
Right. A range with no rule for picking the length would let every start position have 7 primer lengths and 13 probe lengths. That's millions of possible designs, and nothing to choose between them.

The GC rule fixes that. At each start position the designer picks **one** length, the one with GC closest to 50%. So there's still one candidate per position, the same number of choices as now. Each one just gets a better length instead of always 20.

| | Now | Range, no rule | Range + GC rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primer lengths per position | 1 (20) | 7 (18–24) | 1 (chosen by GC) |
| Probe lengths per position | 1 (24) | 13 (18–30) | 1 (chosen by GC) |
| Designs for the N gene | ~100,000 | millions | ~100,000 |

Should I make that change? If two lengths are tied for GC, I'd take the shorter one.

message.content: yes

1	# =============================================================================
2	# PRIMER DESIGN: a qPCR primer pair + probe for a target gene   (version 1)
3	# =============================================================================
4	# 02-120 project: Do early SARS-CoV-2 qPCR primers still match later variants?
5	#
6	# The first model CHECKS primers someone else designed. This file goes the
7	# other way: given a genome and a target gene inside it, it DESIGNS a forward
8	# primer, a reverse primer and a probe, using only what the first model
9	# (first_model_factor_specificity.py) knows about: sequences, the mismatch
10	# allowance, binding sites on both strands, product length, and whether the
11	# probe lies inside the product.
12	#
13	# It does NOT use melting temperature or annealing temperature. It does use
14	# GC content (Section 2b), because G-C pairs hold three hydrogen bonds to A-T's
15	# two: a GC-rich primer binds too strongly, also at sites it only partly
16	# matches, and a GC-rich template folds on itself and copies poorly.
17	#
18	# Inputs:
19	#   genome          - the full genome sequence (a SARS-CoV-2 genome is ~30 kb),
20	#                     plain or FASTA
21	#   target          - the target gene's sequence; it must appear in the genome
22	#                     (on either strand), e.g. the N gene
23	#   max_mismatches  - the mismatch allowance, 0 to MAX_ALLOWED_MISMATCHES (2)
24	#
25	# Output, for each design (best first):
26	#   5'-forward-3', and 3'-reverse-5' (the reverse primer written backwards, so
27	#   it lines up under the genome the way it binds); where each primer binds on
28	#   the genome and its length; the product length; the probe and where it
29	#   binds.
30	#
31	# How it works:
32	#   0. check the target's GC content FIRST: too high -> stop with an error
33	#      and the reason; medium -> carry on, with a warning
34	#   1. find the target in the genome
35	#   2. every PRIMER_LENGTH-base window of the target made of known bases

# PRIMER DESIGN: a qPCR primer pair + probe for a target gene   (version 1)
# =============================================================================
# 02-120 project: Do early SARS-CoV-2 qPCR primers still match later variants?
#
# The first model CHECKS primers someone else designed. This file goes the
# other way: given a genome and a target gene inside it, it DESIGNS a forward
# primer, a reverse primer and a probe, using only what the first model
# (first_model_factor_specificity.py) knows about: sequences, the mismatch
# allowance, binding sites on both strands, product length, and whether the
# probe lies inside the product.

# GC content (Section 2b), because G-C pairs hold three hydrogen bonds to A-T's
# two: a GC-rich primer binds too strongly, also at sites it only partly
# matches, and a GC-rich template folds on itself and copies poorly.
#
# Inputs:
#   genome          - the full genome sequence (a SARS-CoV-2 genome is ~30 kb),
#                     plain or FASTA
#   target          - the target gene's sequence; it must appear in the genome
#                     (on either strand), e.g. the N gene

#      of the gap between them

# window; the reverse primer is the reverse complement of its window (so it

# is written as its + strand window.
#
# Windows with N or ambiguous bases are skipped: the first model cannot say

# =============================================================================

def known(seq):
    return all(base in KNOWN_BASES for base in seq)


def usable(seq):
    """Known bases only, and GC content not too high."""
    return known(seq) and gc_level(seq) != "too high"


def possible_designs(genome, region_start, region_end):
    """Every forward/reverse/probe design inside the target, best first."""
    starts = [s for s in range(region_start, region_end - PRIMER_LENGTH + 1)
              if usable(genome[s:s + PRIMER_LENGTH])]
    designs = []
    for forward_start in starts:
        for reverse_start in starts:
            product_end = reverse_start + PRIMER_LENGTH
            length = product_end - forward_start
            if not PRODUCT_LENGTH[0] <= length <= PRODUCT_LENGTH[1]:
                continue
            gap_start, gap_end = forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH, reverse_start
            if gap_end - gap_start < PROBE_LENGTH:
                continue  # no room for the probe between the primers
            probe_start = gap_start + (gap_end - gap_start - PROBE_LENGTH) // 2
            probe = genome[probe_start:probe_start + PROBE_LENGTH]
            if not usable(probe):
                continue
            medium_gc = [name for name, seq in (
                ("forward", genome[forward_start:forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH]),
                ("reverse", genome[reverse_start:product_end]),
                ("probe", probe)) if gc_level(seq) == "medium"]
            designs.append({
                "forward": {"seq": genome[forward_start:forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH],
                            "start": forward_start, "end": forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH},
                "reverse": {"seq": reverse_complement(genome[reverse_start:product_end]),
                            "start": reverse_start, "end": product_end},
                "probe": {"seq": probe, "start": probe_start,
                          "end": probe_start + PROBE_LENGTH},
                "product_start": forward_start,
                "product_end": product_end,
                "product_length": length,
                "medium_gc": medium_gc,
            })
    designs.sort(key=lambda d: (len(d["medium_gc"]), abs(d["product_length"] - IDEAL_PRODUCT),
                                d["product_start"]))
    return designs


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 4: SPECIFICITY CHECK WITH THE FIRST MODEL
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#   4a. quick screen: each oligo must have exactly one binding site on the
#       whole genome, on either strand, within the mismatch allowance
#       (outcome "binds" or "not assessable" both count as a site). One shared
#       k-mer index; each oligo is checked once even if it is in many designs.
#   4b. full check: run_model on the whole genome must give exactly one
#       product, status "product", at the designed position.
# =============================================================================

def binds_once(oligo, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache):
    if oligo not in cache:
        sites = find_binding_sites("oligo", oligo, genome, index, K, max_mismatches)
        cache[oligo] = len(sites) == 1
    return cache[oligo]


def specific(design, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache):
    """True if the first model finds only the designed product on the whole genome."""
    oligos = (design["forward"]["seq"], design["reverse"]["seq"], design["probe"]["seq"])
    if not all(binds_once(oligo, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache) for oligo in oligos):

def choose_length(genome, anchor, lengths, region_start, region_end, grow):
    """The one window for this anchor: the usable length with GC closest to 50 %.

    grow "right": the window is anchor .. anchor + length (forward primer, probe)
    grow "left":  the window is anchor - length .. anchor (reverse primer)
    Ties go to the shorter length. Returns (start, end), or None if no length works.
    """
    best = None
    for length in range(lengths[0], lengths[1] + 1):
        start, end = (anchor, anchor + length) if grow == "right" else (anchor - length, anchor)
        if start < region_start or end > region_end:
            break
        window = genome[start:end]
        if not usable(window):
            continue
        distance = abs(gc_fraction(window) - IDEAL_GC)
        if best is None or distance < best[0]:   # strictly closer, so ties keep the shorter
            best = (distance, start, end)
    return None if best is None else best[1:]


def all_windows(genome, anchors, lengths, region_start, region_end, grow):
    """{anchor: (start, end)} for every anchor that has a usable length."""
    windows = {}
    for anchor in anchors:
        window = choose_length(genome, anchor, lengths, region_start, region_end, grow)
        if window:
            windows[anchor] = window
    return windows


def centred_probe(probes, gap_start, gap_end):
    """The probe window inside the gap whose middle is closest to the gap's middle."""
    middle = (gap_start + gap_end) / 2
    best = None
    for start in range(gap_start, gap_end - PROBE_LENGTH[0] + 1):
        window = probes.get(start)
        if window is None or window[1] > gap_end:
            continue
        distance = abs((window[0] + window[1]) / 2 - middle)
        if best is None or distance < best[0]:
            best = (distance, window)
    return None if best is None else best[1]


def possible_designs(genome, region_start, region_end):
    """Every forward/reverse/probe design inside the target, best first."""

    """The one window for this anchor: the usable length with GC closest to 50 %.

    grow "left":  the window is anchor - length .. anchor (reverse primer)
    Ties go to the shorter length. Returns (start, end), or None if no length works.
    """
    best = None
    for length in range(lengths[0], lengths[1] + 1):
        start, end = (anchor, anchor + length) if grow == "right" else (anchor - length, anchor)
        if start < region_start or end > region_end:
            break

            continue

        if best is None or distance < best[0]:   # strictly closer, so ties keep the shorter
            best = (distance, start, end)
    return None if best is None else best[1:]

        if window:
            windows[anchor] = window
    return windows

def possible_designs(genome, region_start, region_end):
    """Every forward/reverse/probe design inside the target, best first."""
    starts = [s for s in range(region_start, region_end - PRIMER_LENGTH + 1)
              if usable(genome[s:s + PRIMER_LENGTH])]
    designs = []
    for forward_start in starts:
        for reverse_start in starts:
            product_end = reverse_start + PRIMER_LENGTH
            length = product_end - forward_start
            if not PRODUCT_LENGTH[0] <= length <= PRODUCT_LENGTH[1]:
                continue
            gap_start, gap_end = forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH, reverse_start
            if gap_end - gap_start < PROBE_LENGTH:
                continue  # no room for the probe between the primers
            probe_start = gap_start + (gap_end - gap_start - PROBE_LENGTH) // 2
            probe = genome[probe_start:probe_start + PROBE_LENGTH]
            if not usable(probe):
                continue
            medium_gc = [name for name, seq in (
                ("forward", genome[forward_start:forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH]),
                ("reverse", genome[reverse_start:product_end]),
                ("probe", probe)) if gc_level(seq) == "medium"]
            designs.append({
                "forward": {"seq": genome[forward_start:forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH],
                            "start": forward_start, "end": forward_start + PRIMER_LENGTH},
                "reverse": {"seq": reverse_complement(genome[reverse_start:product_end]),
                            "start": reverse_start, "end": product_end},
                "probe": {"seq": probe, "start": probe_start,
                          "end": probe_start + PROBE_LENGTH},
                "product_start": forward_start,
                "product_end": product_end,
                "product_length": length,
                "medium_gc": medium_gc,
            })

def choose_length(genome, anchor, lengths, region_start, region_end, grow):
    """The one window for this anchor: the usable length with GC closest to 50 %.

    grow "right": the window is anchor .. anchor + length (forward primer, probe)
    grow "left":  the window is anchor - length .. anchor (reverse primer)
    Ties go to the shorter length. Returns (start, end), or None if no length works.
    """
    best = None
    for length in range(lengths[0], lengths[1] + 1):
        start, end = (anchor, anchor + length) if grow == "right" else (anchor - length, anchor)
        if start < region_start or end > region_end:
            break
        window = genome[start:end]
        if not usable(window):
            continue
        distance = abs(gc_fraction(window) - IDEAL_GC)
        if best is None or distance < best[0]:   # strictly closer, so ties keep the shorter
            best = (distance, start, end)
    return None if best is None else best[1:]


def all_windows(genome, anchors, lengths, region_start, region_end, grow):
    """{anchor: (start, end)} for every anchor that has a usable length."""
    windows = {}
    for anchor in anchors:
        window = choose_length(genome, anchor, lengths, region_start, region_end, grow)
        if window:
            windows[anchor] = window
    return windows


def centred_probe(probes, gap_start, gap_end):
    """The probe window inside the gap whose middle is closest to the gap's middle."""
    middle = (gap_start + gap_end) / 2
    best = None
    for start in range(gap_start, gap_end - PROBE_LENGTH[0] + 1):
        window = probes.get(start)
        if window is None or window[1] > gap_end:
            continue
        distance = abs((window[0] + window[1]) / 2 - middle)
        if best is None or distance < best[0]:
            best = (distance, window)
    return None if best is None else best[1]


def possible_designs(genome, region_start, region_end):
    """Every forward/reverse/probe design inside the target, best first."""
    # forward and probe: anchored at their 5' end (left), grow right
    forwards = all_windows(genome, range(region_start, region_end), PRIMER_LENGTH,
                           region_start, region_end, "right")
    probes = all_windows(genome, range(region_start, region_end), PROBE_LENGTH,
                         region_start, region_end, "right")
    # reverse: anchored at its 5' end, which is the window's RIGHT end; grows left
    reverses = all_windows(genome, range(region_start + 1, region_end + 1), PRIMER_LENGTH,
                           region_start, region_end, "left")

    designs = []
    for forward_start, (_, forward_end) in forwards.items():
        for product_end in range(forward_start + PRODUCT_LENGTH[0],
                                 forward_start + PRODUCT_LENGTH[1] + 1):
            if product_end not in reverses:
                continue
            reverse_start = reverses[product_end][0]
            if reverse_start - forward_end < PROBE_LENGTH[0]:
                continue  # no room for the probe between the primers
            probe_window = centred_probe(probes, forward_end, reverse_start)
            if probe_window is None:
                continue
            forward = genome[forward_start:forward_end]
            reverse_window = genome[reverse_start:product_end]
            probe = genome[probe_window[0]:probe_window[1]]
            medium_gc = [name for name, seq in (
                ("forward", forward), ("reverse", reverse_window), ("probe", probe))
                if gc_level(seq) == "medium"]
            designs.append({
                "forward": {"seq": forward, "start": forward_start, "end": forward_end},
                "reverse": {"seq": reverse_complement(reverse_window),
                            "start": reverse_start, "end": product_end},
                "probe": {"seq": probe, "start": probe_window[0], "end": probe_window[1]},
                "product_start": forward_start,
                "product_end": product_end,
                "product_length": product_end - forward_start,
                "medium_gc": medium_gc,
            })

# The mismatch allowance is capped at 2. The first model finds sites with

# the CDC probes are 23-24).

# A range alone would give every position 7 primer lengths and 13 probe
# lengths, so millions of designs and nothing to choose between them. Each
# position therefore gets ONE length: the one whose GC content is closest to
# IDEAL_GC (50 %), the shorter one on a tie (Section 3, choose_length).
#
# The mismatch allowance is capped at 2. The first model finds sites with
# k = 6 base seeds, and needs (oligo length) // (allowance + 1) >= 6, so the
# shortest oligo, 18 bases, can use at most 2 (#15, #40). A higher allowance
# could miss off-target sites without warning.
# =============================================================================

IDEAL_GC = 0.50             # each oligo's length is chosen to get closest to this
PRIMER_LENGTH = (18, 24)
PROBE_LENGTH = (18, 30)

The designer now picks primer lengths from 18–24 and probe lengths from 18–30, and all 12 tests pass after I updated them.

**How it chooses a length.** For each start position the designer picks one length: the one with GC content closest to 50%, taking the shorter length on a tie. So there's still one candidate per position: about 100,000 possible designs for the N gene, the same as before. The demo now takes about 2 seconds instead of under 1.

On the N gene, the designs now use 18–23-base primers and 18–30-base probes, with GC between 46.7% and 55%.

**What changed in the tests** (`test_primer_design.py`)
- The length checks now accept the ranges instead of exactly 20 and 24.
- **Case 2**, re-worked by hand:
  - The forward primer is 18 bases. At 50% GC it ties with 20, 22 and 24, and 18 is the shortest.
  - The reverse primer is 22 bases. It's the shortest length at exactly 50%; 24 ties.
  - The probe is centred in the gap between them.
- **Case 8** needed a new near-copy. With 18-base primers, "every 10th base changed" can leave a primer covering only one change. Now every 12th base is changed, so any 18–24-base primer covers 1 or 2 changes:
  - Allowance 2: no design, because every primer also binds the copy.
  - Allowance 0: 3 designs.

**CDC check, rerun.** It's still not reproducing the published primers, for the reason we expected: it keeps preferring 100 bp products starting at the first base of the target. The second choice is getting close for two assays:
- **N2:** the designer's second design is also 67 bp. Its forward primer (29214–29233) starts right after the published reverse site ends at 29230.
- **N3:** the second design is 72 bp, and its forward primer starts at 28731, one base from where the published reverse site starts (28732).

There's a side effect: the 50% rule often chooses 18 bases, the shortest length, whenever that already hits 50%. Without Tm, nothing pushes it toward longer primers.

Next would be setting the ideal product to about 70 bp and reporting where each CDC design ranks. Nothing is committed yet. When we commit, I'll add #53 to Log 11 and update `test_cases_primer_design.txt` with the new positions and sequences.

Before I build the ranking, I need to pin down what "best match" and "flagged" mean, because the GC change affects both.

**"Best match":** every design is copied straight from the target, so all primers match it perfectly. Which of these did you mean?
- **(A) Closest to the ideal:** GC of the forward, reverse and probe closest to 50%, and product length closest to the ideal. This is my suggestion.
- **(B) Most specific:** the primers' nearest look-alike sites elsewhere in the genome have the most mismatches. That makes them least likely to stick to the wrong place. It's all first-model information, but slower to compute.

**"Flagged":** once primers must be 40–60% GC, no single primer can get a GC flag any more. The only warning left is the target-level one (target above 60% or below 40%), and it applies to every design equally. So a design-level flag needs something else to trigger it.     gc = gc_fraction(seq)
    if gc > GC_TOO_HIGH_ABOVE:

    if gc > GC_MEDIUM_ABOVE:

def binds_once(oligo, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache):
    if oligo not in cache:
        sites = find_binding_sites("oligo", oligo, genome, index, K, max_mismatches)
        cache[oligo] = len(sites) == 1
    return cache[oligo]


def specific(design, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache):
    """True if the first model finds only the designed product on the whole genome."""
    oligos = (design["forward"]["seq"], design["reverse"]["seq"], design["probe"]["seq"])
    if not all(binds_once(oligo, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache) for oligo in oligos):
        return False
    result = run_model(oligos[0], oligos[1], genome, probe=oligos[2],
                       max_mismatches=max_mismatches, k=K)
    products = result["products"]
    return (len(products) == 1 and products[0]["status"] == "product"
            and products[0]["start"] == design["product_start"]
            and products[0]["end"] == design["product_end"])

# =============================================================================

def design_primers(genome, target, max_mismatches=2, designs_wanted=DESIGNS_WANTED):
    """Design up to designs_wanted primer pairs + probes for target, best first."""
    genome, target = clean_sequence(genome), clean_sequence(target)
    if not 0 <= max_mismatches <= MAX_ALLOWED_MISMATCHES:
        raise ValueError(f"mismatch allowance must be 0 to {MAX_ALLOWED_MISMATCHES}")
    if len(target) < PRODUCT_LENGTH[0]:
        raise ValueError(f"the target must be at least {PRODUCT_LENGTH[0]} bases long")

    # -- the GC check comes first: a too GC-rich target stops here
    warnings = []
    target_warning = check_target_gc(target)
    if target_warning:
        warnings.append(target_warning)

    region_start, region_end, strand = find_target(genome, target)
    designs = possible_designs(genome, region_start, region_end)

    index = build_kmer_index(genome, K)
    cache, chosen, checked = {}, [], 0
    for design in designs:
        if len(chosen) == designs_wanted:
            break
        # each design's product must not overlap an earlier one's, so the
        # options cover different parts of the gene
        if any(design["product_start"] < d["product_end"] and d["product_start"] < design["product_end"]
               for d in chosen):
            continue
        checked += 1
        if specific(design, genome, index, max_mismatches, cache):
            chosen.append(design)

    for number, design in enumerate(chosen, 1):
        for name in design["medium_gc"]:
            seq = design[name]["seq"]
            warnings.append(f"design {number}: {name} GC content is {gc_percent(seq)} "
                            f"(medium): it may bind more strongly than intended")

    return {
        "warnings": warnings,
        "target": {"start": region_start, "end": region_end, "strand": strand},
        "possible": len(designs),
        "checked": checked,
        "designs": chosen,
    }

def print_designs(result, max_mismatches):

content.text:
The 40–60% GC rule and the best-match ranking are both in, and all 14 tests pass.

**GC rule**
- **Primers and probe:** every oligo must be 40–60% GC; anything outside is never used. Within that range, each oligo's length is the one closest to 50%, as before.
- **Target gene:** still checked first, before anything else runs.
  - Above 70%: error.
  - 60–70%: warning.
  - Below 40%: warning only, since SARS-CoV-2 as a whole is about 38% GC.
- **No usable stretches:** if the target has no 40–60% stretches at all, it returns no designs, and a warning says GC is the reason.

**Ranking: best match first.** Each design gets a match penalty, and lower is better:
```
penalty = |forward GC − 50| + |reverse GC − 50| + |probe GC − 50|   (percentage points)
        + |product length − 100| / 10
```
So 1 point is 1 GC percentage point on one oligo, or 10 bp of product length. Designs come out in penalty order, and each one shows its penalty.

There's no "then not-flagged" step. With every oligo now inside 40–60%, no design can carry its own flag. The only warnings left are about the whole target, and those apply to every design equally. If you think of something that should flag a single design, I can add it as the second sort key.

**Tests: 14 cases, all pass**
- **Case 2 (ranking):** a hand example. A design with GC 45%, 50% and 55% and an 80 bp product scores 5 + 0 + 5 + 2 = 12. It also checks that designs come out in penalty order.
- **Case 12 (new):** a target at about 33% GC gives the low warning and still returns designs.
- **Case 13 (new):** an `ATTA` repeat target (0% GC) gives no designs, and the warning names GC as the reason.

**CDC check.** The published N1–N3 primers all pass the 40–60% rule (40.0–58.3%), so the designer could have chosen them. It still prefers 100 bp products, but **N2 came close**. Its reverse primer is `ATGCGCGACATTCCGAAGAA` (29213–29232). That's the CDC reverse primer `GCGCGACATTCCGAAGAA` with 2 extra bases on its 5' end, chosen because the longer one is closer to 50% GC.

On the N gene, many designs now tie at a perfect 0.0, so the earliest start breaks the tie. Setting the ideal product to about 70 bp would probably bring the designer closer to the CDC designs. That's the next step on your list.

Nothing is committed yet. When we commit, I'll add #53 (length ranges) and #54 (the GC rule and ranking) to the diary and documentation, and update `test_cases_primer_design.txt`.

content.text:
You can now set the product length. It defaults to 100 bp, and designs are made within ± 50 bp of whatever you choose. All 15 tests pass.

**How to use it**
- In Python: `design_primers(genome, target, 2, 70)`.
- From the command line: `python3 journal/primer_design.py genome.fasta target.fasta 2 70`.
- The last two numbers are the mismatch allowance and the product length, and both can be left out.

**Limits I set**
- **Shortest: 54 bp.** That's the minimum that fits an 18-base forward primer, an 18-base probe and an 18-base reverse primer. Anything shorter gives an error with that reason.
- **Longest: the target's length.** A longer request gives an error saying the target is too short for that product.
- **Outside 60–150 bp:** still designs, with the warning "a 300 bp product is outside 60–150 bp, where qPCR works best".
- **Off-target products:** when it checks for products elsewhere in the genome, `run_model` now looks for ones at least as long as the requested product. Before, it would have missed any longer than 1000 bp.

**Tested on the N gene:** asking for 70, 300 or 1000 bp gave designs of exactly that length, in 1–3 seconds.

**New test case 14:**
- At 70 bp: the best design is exactly 70 bp, every design follows every rule, and there's no warning.
- At 300 bp: designs are 250–350 bp, and the qPCR warning appears.

Case 15, bad input, now covers a product length of 53 and a target too short for the product.

**CDC check at 70 bp:** the designs are now the right size (70 bp, against the CDC's 67–72), but the primers still sit in different places:
- **N1:** the designer's forward primer starts at 28275, 12 bases before the CDC one.
- **N2:** its forward primer overlaps where the CDC probe sits.
- **N3:** its reverse primer sits on the CDC forward site.

Many designs score a perfect 0 (exactly 50% GC, exactly 70 bp), so the earliest start wins the tie. The CDC primers are at 40–58% GC, so our ranking scores them a little worse than those perfect designs. With only GC and length to go on, the designer has no reason to prefer the CDC positions.

Nothing is committed yet. The diary, documentation and test cases file still need entries for this session's changes: the length ranges, the 40–60% GC rule and ranking, and the product length setting.

TEST CASES: PRIMER DESIGN (version 2)
======================================
Designer: journal/primer_design.py
Tests:    journal/test_primer_design.py
Run:      python3 journal/test_primer_design.py   (15 cases)
Real-data check: CDC N1/N2/N3 (see the end of this file)

The designer takes a genome, a target gene inside it, a mismatch allowance
(0-2) and a product length (default 100 bp), and returns up to 3 designs: a
forward primer, a reverse primer and a probe. It uses only what the first
model uses (sequence, mismatch allowance, binding sites on both strands,
product length, probe inside the product), plus GC content. No melting or
annealing temperature.

Fake genome (the same every run: seeded random bases):
  2,000 random bases (seed 1, 50 % GC)
  + 400-base target (seed 3, 45.3 % GC)
  + 2,000 random bases (seed 2, 50 % GC)
  Target = genome positions 2001-2400 (1-based)
  Target starts GCATGCTGGTAGGTTTCAACCTCTTAATAATGTGGCAGCTAGGTCGTGTCATGTTATGCT...

Rules every returned design must follow (checked for every design):
  - forward = the genome window; reverse = reverse complement of its window;
    probe = the genome window
  - primers 18-24 bases, probe 18-30 bases, all inside the target
  - each oligo's length = the one with GC closest to 50 % (shorter on a tie)
  - every primer and probe 40-60 % GC
  - probe between the primers, overlapping neither
  - product within +/- 50 bp of the chosen length (never below 54 bp)
  - independent check: run_model (first model) on the whole genome with the
    designed oligos finds exactly ONE product, status "product", at the
    designed place

Ranking, best match first:
  penalty = |forward GC - 50| + |reverse GC - 50| + |probe GC - 50|
            (percentage points)  +  |product - chosen length| / 10
  Lower is better; ties go to the earlier start. Each later design's product
  must not overlap an earlier one.

31	## Log 1 · 2026-10-29 · Version 1: First model, factor: specificity
32	
33	**Commit:** `8e3f1c3`
34	
35	**Technical overview.** Specificity only: no melting temperature, no real data.
36	- `build_kmer_index` maps every k-mer (k = 5) of the target to its positions.
37	- `find_binding_sites` seeds by the pigeonhole principle: a primer split into
38	  (max_mismatches + 1) pieces has at least one exact piece at any true site.
39	  Each seed hit is then checked over the full primer, on both strands (the
40	  "-" strand by searching the primer's reverse complement).
41	- `distances_from_3prime` reports mismatches as distance from the 3' end
42	  (1 = 3'-terminal base); the 3' end is the right end of a "+" site and the
43	  left end of a "-" site.
44	- `pair_into_products` pairs each "+" site with each downstream "-" site
45	  within `min_length`–`max_length` (default 20–1000 bp).
46	- Tests: 7 hand-solvable cases on fake 16-base primers and a poly-A-padded
47	  fake target.
48	
49	**#1. Problem:** stating the seeding limit:
50	(primer length) // (max_mismatches + 1) must be ≥ k.
51	
52	---
53	
54	## Log 2 · 2026-10-29 · Version 2: Handling bad sequencing data
55	
56	**Commits:** `81d909e`, `504d494`
57	
58	**Technical overview.** Read alignment (Salmon, STAR, TopHat) is not needed:
59	the genomes are finished NCBI consensus sequences. Poor sequencing still
60	leaves N bases and missing ends in them. GC content was rejected as a quality
61	signal (FASTA has no quality scores; SARS-CoV-2 has real AT-rich regions).
62	
63	**#2. Problem:** an N in the genome was counted as a mismatch, so missing data
64	looked like a mutation and a primer could be wrongly reported as lost.
65	**Fix:** `compare_site` replaces `mismatch_offsets` and returns mismatches and
66	unknown positions separately; unknowns never count toward the allowance. New
67	`primer_outcome` / `assay_outcome` give three outcomes: binds, mismatched,
68	not assessable.
69	
70	**#3. Problem:** primer sites that ran off the start or end of a sequence were
71	never found.
72	**Fix:** `candidate_starts` adds every placement hanging off either end
73	(positions outside the sequence count as unknown) and every placement
74	overlapping an N, since k-mer seeds can't land on Ns. Such sites are "not
75	assessable" with the reason "runs off the start/end of the sequence".
76	
77	**#4. Problem** (found while fixing #2): a long run of Ns would make every
78	primer "not assessable".
79	**Fix:** a not-assessable site needs at least `MIN_KNOWN_BASES` = 10 known
80	bases within the allowance.
81	
82	**#5. Problem:** no plain-language record of what each test checks.
83	**Fix:** `test_cases_specificity.txt`, with every case's exact target,
84	outcome and meaning. Tests added: Cases 7-10 (Ns in a site, cut end, cut
85	start, real mismatches next to missing data).
86	
87	**#6. Problem:** the bad-data note in the code was titled "NOTE TO READERS".
88	**Fix:** renamed "HANDLING BAD SEQUENCING DATA".
89	
90	---
91	
92	## Log 3 · 2026-10-30 · Version 3: Explaining failures
93	
94	**Commit:** `fcf677c`
95	
96	**Technical overview.** `run_model` replaces `predict_products` and returns
97	one result: `sites`, `products` (each with a `status`), `outcomes`,
98	`near_misses`, `assay`, `warnings`.
99	
100	**#7. Problem:** logic bug. In Case 10 the reverse primer could not bind
101	anywhere, yet the assay was "not assessable" only because of an N in the
102	forward site.
103	**Fix:** `pair_into_products` now pairs "binds" and "not assessable" sites
104	into possible products, and `product_status` labels each one. The assay is
105	"not assessable" only when a possible product depends on missing data;
106	otherwise "no product".
107	
108	**#8. Problem:** a 3' mismatch counted the same as a 5' one, although 3'
109	mismatches are the ones that block extension.
110	**Fix:** sites with a mismatch within `THREE_PRIME_WINDOW` = 3 bases of the
111	3' end are flagged, and their products produce a warning (new
112	`3' END RISK WINDOW` banner).
113	
114	**#9. Problem:** the qPCR probe was ignored, although a product gives no
115	signal unless the probe binds inside it.
116	**Fix:** optional `probe` argument; `probe_inside` checks for probe sites
117	fully inside each product. Primers binding without the probe give the new
118	assay outcome "no signal". Assay priority: product > not assessable >
119	no signal > no product.
120	
121	**#10. Problem:** degenerate primer bases (e.g. the Y in the CDC N3 probe)
122	were counted as mismatches and could not be used as seeds.
123	**Fix:** an `IUPAC` table; `base_matches` accepts any base a letter stands
124	for, and `expand_degenerate` / `seed_hits` look up every plain k-mer a
125	degenerate seed stands for. `clean_oligo` rejects non-DNA letters.
126	
127	**#11. Problem:** mismatches gave only a position, not the base change.
128	**Fix:** `describe_changes` reports "primer C, genome G", both bases in the
129	primer's 5'→3' direction (complemented for "-" sites).
130	
131	**#12. Problem:** a failed primer gave no clue where it almost bound, and
132	insertions/deletions (e.g. Alpha's spike Δ69–70) looked like many mismatches.
133	**Fix:** `find_near_miss` runs for every "mismatched" oligo. It anchors on
134	every exact k-mer the primer shares with the genome, then `placements` /
135	`gapped_pairs` try no gap or one gap of up to `MAX_INDEL` = 6 bases.
136	Score = substitutions + 1 per gap (one event). The best placement is reported
137	with its changes and gap, or "none close".
138	
139	**#13. Problem:** positions were 0-based, unlike the CDC table and genome
140	browsers.
141	**Fix:** stored 0-based, printed 1-based by `print_report`.
142	
143	**#14. Problem:** untested edge cases.
144	**Fix:** Cases 11-19 (self-pairing, overlapping sites, allowance too high →
145	`ValueError`, palindromic primer, degenerate base, probe binds / fails,
146	insertion, deletion).
147	
148	### Found while building version 3
149	
150	**#15. Problem:** near-miss anchoring needs one exact 5-base stretch. In
151	Case 10 three mismatches 4 bases apart leave none, so nothing was found.
152	**Fix:** documented as a limit; Case 10 expects "none close". A 16-base primer
153	is always found with ≤ 2 events, a 20-base primer with ≤ 3.
154	
155	**#16. Problem:** on a random 30,000-base sequence, a CDC primer got a fake
156	"6-base deletion + 1 mismatch" near-miss: a long deletion leaves few bases to
157	compare, so chance matches are easy.
158	**Fix:** `MIN_MATCHED_BASES` = 14 primer bases must match exactly.
159	
160	**#17. Problem:** chance matches still appeared (a deletion + 2–3 mismatches),
161	because a gap can sit in many places.
162	**Fix:** `NEAR_MISS_MAX_EVENTS_WITH_INDEL` = 2 (the gap + ≤ 1 substitution);
163	`NEAR_MISS_MAX_EVENTS` = 4 without a gap. Result: 0 false near-misses on 10
164	random genomes; a planted 6-base deletion in a 20-base primer is still found.
165	A 16-base primer can therefore show deletions of ≤ 2 bases: Case 18 changed
166	from a 4-base to a 2-base deletion, and Case 18b (6 bases, refused) was added.
167	
168	---

170	## Log 4 · 2026-10-30 · Version 4: Smarter logic and the first real data
171	
172	**Commit:** `8af20dc`
173	
174	**Technical overview.** Four logic fixes, the first real-data check, tests
175	that verify the search itself, and the model and tests split into two files.
176	
177	**#18. Problem:** "not assessable" was too cautious. With 2 mismatches
178	allowed, a site with 0 mismatches + 1 N binds whatever the N is, but was
179	reported "not assessable".
180	**Fix:** in `find_binding_sites`, if mismatches + unknowns ≤ max_mismatches,
181	the outcome is "binds" with the reason "binds even if every unknown base is a
182	mismatch". Case 7b added; in Case 10 the forward primer now binds.
183	
184	**#19. Problem:** genome ambiguity codes were all treated like N. A genome R
185	(A or G) can never match a primer C.
186	**Fix:** `genome_vs_primer` returns match (every option accepted), mismatch
187	(no option accepted) or unknown (some accepted); `compare_site` uses it.
188	Case 20 added.

190	**#20. Problem:** mismatches were all-or-nothing; a mild G–T counted the same
191	as a severe C–C.
192	**Fix:** `mismatch_severity` grades primer–template pairs A–A, G–A, A–G and
193	C–C as severe and all others as mild (Stadhouders et al. 2010; Kwok et al.

196	(unknown in window); `worst_risk` combines a product's two sites. The
197	allowance still counts each mismatch as 1, keeping the seeding guarantee.
198	Case 3b updated, Case 21 added.

201	near the 5' end usually still extends.
202	**Fix:** `find_indel_sites` adds "binds" sites with one gap of
203	≤ `MAX_BINDING_INDEL` = 1 base, more than half the primer length from the 3'
204	end. The gap counts as 1 mismatch, and placements overlapping an existing
205	ungapped site are skipped. Shared helpers `anchors_for` and `describe_indel`
206	were factored out of `find_near_miss`. Case 22 added.
207	
208	**#22. Problem:** the model had never been run on real data.
209	**Fix:** `cdc_reference_check.py` (`read_assays`, `check_viral_assay`,
210	`check_negative_control`) runs N1, N2, N3 with probes and the RNase P control
211	on NC_045512.2 (`read_fasta`). Allowance 2. Results: one product per N assay

213	N3's degenerate probe), and no RP product.

215	**#23. Problem** (found by #22): N1 comes out at 72 bp, but the table lists
216	73 bp. The table's own published (28303–28374) and verified (28287–28358)
217	coordinates both span 72 bases.
218	**Status: RESOLVED in #36** (the table's 73 was wrong; 72 is correct).
219	
220	**#24. Problem:** nothing proved the fast k-mer search finds every site.
221	**Fix:** Case 23 compares plain sites with `brute_force_sites` (every start
222	position, both strands, same classification rules) on 200 random 300-base
223	targets × allowances 0–2, with mutated primer copies, N/Y bases and cut ends.
224	Identical on all 600 searches (1,361 sites).
225	
226	**#25. Problem:** the random-genome check from #17 was only run by hand.
227	**Fix:** saved as Case 24 (CDC N1 primers + probe on a random 30,000-base
228	sequence: no sites, no near-misses).
229	
230	**#26. Problem:** the model and tests shared one ~1,000-line file.
231	**Fix:** tests moved to `test_first_model_factor_specificity.py`, which
232	imports the model. `read_fasta` added to the model for real genomes.

234	**#27. Problem:** the report read "deletion of 1 bases (primer bases 15-15 …)".
235	**Fix:** `format_indel` now writes "deletion of 1 base (primer base 15 from 3' …)".

323	lineage change, not an isolate quirk. No code changed.

325	severity and `three_prime_risk` are labels only. The binds/product decision
326	uses the mismatch count alone, so a severe 3' mismatch still gives
327	"product" with a `[3' RISK: HIGH]` warning.

331	## Log 7 · 2026-11-09 · Realistic test primers and k = 6
332	
333	**Commit:** `0e0e449`
334	
335	**Note:** most primers used in real (biological) PCR and qPCR are 18-30
336	bases long: long enough to be unique in a genome and to anneal at about
337	55-65 °C, short enough to bind quickly and cheaply. The CDC SARS-CoV-2
338	primers and probes are 18-24 bases. The tests and k = 6 are built around
339	this range.
340	
341	**#38. Problem:** every hand-solvable test used 16-base fake primers, shorter
342	than real qPCR primers (18-30 bases; the CDC ones are 18-24). The 16 was never
343	justified; it was simply the longest length that fit k = 5 with 2 mismatches
344	(16 // 3 = 5).
345	**Fix:** `test_first_model_factor_specificity.py` rebuilt on two fake sets:
346	set A (`FORWARD_A` 20, `REVERSE_A` 24, `PROBE_A` 26 bases; 70 bp amplicon,
347	used by most cases) and set B (`FORWARD_B` 18, `REVERSE_B` 30 bases; 73 bp
348	amplicon, for length cases), plus an 18-base `PALINDROME` and a 20-base
349	`OVERLAP_REVERSE`. Every expected answer was redone by hand. Changes beyond
350	the numbers:
351	- Case 1b (new): exact match with set B, 73 bp.
352	- Cases 3, 3c, 21a: the planted 3' and 5' mismatches are now A-C (mild).
353	- Case 10: 4 mismatches 5 apart are needed to hide a 24-base site from the
354	  near-miss search (3 always leave a long enough stretch).
355	- Case 13: the error now comes from the 18-base primer (18 // 4 = 4).
356	- Case 18b now uses the 18-base primer (6-base deletion leaves 12 < 14
357	  matched bases, "none close"); new Case 18c finds the same 6-base deletion in
358	  the 30-base primer (24 bases still match). Whether a deletion is recognised
359	  depends on primer length.
360	- Case 22b: the 3'-half deletion moved to 4 from the 3' end; at 2 or 3 the
361	  neighbouring Cs made it look like 0 or 1 mismatch.
362	- Case 23 now checks primers of 18, 20, 24 and 30 bases (600 searches agree
363	  with the brute-force search, 1129 sites).
364	`test_cases_specificity.txt` rewritten with the new targets and markers;
365	the model's comments no longer use 16-base examples.
366	
367	**#39. Problem:** k = 5 was a leftover of the 16-base test primers. With real
368	primers of 18 bases or more, a longer seed is allowed and much faster: a
369	random 6-mer hits about 7 places in a 30,000-base genome, a 5-mer about 29.
370	**Fix:** `run_model` default `k=6`, with the reason written above
371	`build_kmer_index`. The seeding rule (length // (max_mismatches + 1) >= k)
372	now needs at least 18 bases with the default 2 mismatches; every CDC oligo
373	qualifies (shortest: N2 reverse, 18). The tests take ~10 s instead of
374	~18 s. `cdc_reference_check.py` and `variant_check.py` give identical results
375	with k = 5 and k = 6.
376	
377	**#40. Problem:** the near-miss and small-gap searches also start from exact
378	k-base stretches, so k = 6 weakens them: a near-miss is now guaranteed with
379	up to 2 events for 18- and 20-base primers (3 for 24, 4 for 30), down from 3
380	for a 20-base primer with k = 5.
381	**Fix:** documented as a limit (Section 5 comment) and shown by new Case
382	10b: 3 mismatches cut the 20-base forward site into exact stretches of
383	5, 5, 5 and 2 bases; with k = 6 the near-miss is "none close", with `k=5` it
384	is found (3 events, 3, 9 and 15 from the 3' end).

388	## Log 8 · 2026-11-09 · 3' risk changes the result; a mislabelled genome
389	
390	**Commit:** `e6793bf`
391	
392	**#41. Problem:** a severe mismatch at a primer's 3' end only printed a
393	warning; the product still counted as a plain "product" (#37), so a pair
394	likely to amplify poorly looked as good as a perfect one.
395	**Fix:** new product status **"at risk"**: both primers bind (and the probe,
396	if given), but a primer site has `three_prime_risk` "high" (a severe mismatch
397	within `THREE_PRIME_WINDOW` = 3 bases of the 3' end). `product_status`
398	returns it after the "no signal" and "not assessable" checks. The new
399	`STATUS_ORDER` = product > at risk > not assessable > no signal > no product
400	is used by `assay_outcome` and is meant to rank primer pairs on the future
401	website (at-risk pairs flagged and suggested last). LOW and POSSIBLE risk do
402	not change the status. The probe's 3' risk is ignored: a TaqMan probe is
403	never extended. Warnings now cover "at risk" products too;
404	`cdc_reference_check.py` and `variant_check.py` count "at risk" products as
405	products. Case 3b now expects "at risk"; new Case 3d (two copies, one with
406	the severe 3' mismatch) gives two "at risk" products and one "product", and

411	signature positions it carries all of Beta's (B.1.351) changes (D80A
412	A21801C, D215G, K417N, E484K, N501Y, Δ242-244) and none of Alpha's (ΔH69/V70,

418	(`variant_check.py` now labels it "Beta"; its header comment flags the

424	(`af9073fb-….jsonl`) includes a 15-question quiz on the model plus review

426	- 3' risk uses `from_3prime <= THREE_PRIME_WINDOW`, so 1–3 bases from the
427	  3' end are inside the window.

429	- Status is decided in the order mismatch count, then window, then severity.
430	- The 1-base indel rule (`from_3prime[0] > length // 2`) is separate from
